open_points.subject: A28 clock-reading scope
open_points.text: “the wall clock gives the instant: … one reading per request … (no cache … no second reading)” conflicts with “An operation reads the clock once for its own timestamps”, the audit-writer exception that “the writer takes it when it appends”, and the carried rule that each reading remains “at the same point of the same operation.”
open_points.question: Is a wall-clock value read and shared once across an entire HTTP request, or does each guard, owning use case, and audit append perform its own operation-level reading through system_clock? How is the rule applied to non-HTTP operations such as bootstrap?
options: One wall reading is shared by every component participating in an HTTP request, with a separately specified audit exception and an equivalent operation scope for CLI work
Each independently defined operation reads system_clock once, so one HTTP request may cause several wall readings
“Per request” means per call to utc_now, leaving operation-level consumers independent
open_points.default_guess: Preserve the stated carried behavior: each operation-level consumer calls system_clock once at its former read point, and audit_writer takes its separate reading.

witness.initial: An authenticated mutation will create a business record and append its significant-action audit; the host wall clock advances between the use case and audit append.
events: authorization_guard reads the current instant while authorizing the request
the owning use case reads the instant used for its business timestamps
outcomes: A request-wide interpretation supplies one shared wall value, except to whatever audit exception the implementer infers, so business and audit timestamps may be equal.
An operation-level interpretation performs separate system_clock calls at the preserved points, so the audit occurred_at can be later than the business timestamp.
witness.observer: A reader of the persisted business and audit records, and tests asserting clock-call counts

set_aside.subject: rejection of OCR provider, confidence, and raw fields
set_aside.text: The new INV-031 check requires a “provider-carrying result” to be “refused at decoding, by create_expense_from_recognition and over HTTP”, while `models` owns request models and their local validators, `api` owns request-body decoding, and `expense_intake` owns “rejection of provider and raw fields” but receives typed portal models from which such forbidden fields may already be absent.
set_aside.question: Which module owns detecting forbidden OCR fields, and what input reaches create_expense_from_recognition so that it can itself reject a provider-carrying result after decoding has already rejected that shape?
options: models/API decoding exclusively rejects unknown OCR fields; expense_intake receives only the closed accepted DTO
expense_intake receives a boundary shape that can represent forbidden provider/confidence/raw fields and owns their rejection
Both layers validate them, with explicitly distinct raw and decoded input types and ownership
set_aside.default_guess: Use an explicit raw boundary DTO whose strict decoding is owned by models/API, then let expense_intake own only semantic projection of the accepted closed DTO.

witness.initial: The database contains no expense for recognized_document_id R.
events: A caller submits an otherwise valid confirmed-recognition payload containing an extra provider field
api decodes the body and would call create_expense_from_recognition
outcomes: A strict request model rejects the field before the use case, so expense_intake cannot perform the rejection attributed to it.
A permissive decoder drops the field and expense_intake accepts and persists the expense unless it is given the raw payload or another field-preserving shape.
witness.observer: The HTTP caller, the expense table, and the INV-031 verification check
